text: This is the fast revision of Lectures 1 to 10, built for one goal: solving mid sem and quiz questions quickly, with every formula in your head, because you cannot carry a sheet.

Each lecture gets one scene: its circuit on the left and every exam formula on the right, one at a time. Say each formula with the voice. Then an if the question says box tells you which formula a question is asking for.
Every few lectures, rapid-fire questions with a tight clock. At the end, a formula sprint. Use Memorise pace if you want longer pauses.
Square law: I D equals half mu C ox W over L V overdrive squared, and the overdrive is V G S minus V threshold.
G M three ways. The fastest in exams is 2 I D over V overdrive.
R O equals 1 over ( lambda I D ), and the intrinsic gain G M R O equals 2 over ( lambda V overdrive ).
Saturated: N mos drain at least V threshold below its gate; P mos drain at most V threshold above.
And for every design question, the square law turned round: W over L equals 2 I D over ( mu C ox V overdrive squared ).
If a question asks for W over L: find the current and the overdrive first. For G M: two I D over V overdrive. For is it saturated: the fence.
Every number in this course comes from one transistor. Five formulas.
G M equals 2 I D over V overdrive, R O equals 1 over ( lambda I D ).
W over L equals 2 I D over ( mu C ox V overdrive squared ).
Into a drain: R O. With R S under the source it multiplies: about G M R O R S. Up multiplies.
Into a source: about 1 over G M. Down divides.
A cascode: G M 2 R O 2 R O 1, so its gain is about g M r O, squared.
Every gain: G M times R up in parallel with R down.
Mirrors copy current in the ratio of the W over L values.
Any gain question: look up, look down, parallel them, times G M. Any current question: mirror ratios.
The second toolkit: what resistance you see looking into each terminal, and how every gain is built from it.
Up multiplies: G M R O R S. Down divides: 1 over G M.
A. V equals G M ( R up in parallel with R down ).
The divider sets beta equals R 2 over ( R 1 plus R 2 ), and the ideal gain is 1 over beta.
The real gain is A. over (1 plus beta A.), a little below 1 over beta.
The gain error: 1 over (1 plus beta A.), about 1 over ( beta A.).
So the minimum open-loop gain is the closed-loop gain divided by the allowed error.
Gain error below some percent: the open-loop gain must be at least the ideal gain divided by the error.
Lecture 1, Razavi Example 9.1: why an op amp needs a huge open-loop gain.
A. closed equals A. over 1 plus beta A., epsilon is about 1 over beta A.
One pole: G B W is A. zero times the pole, and the pole is the output resistance times C L.
Gain of both: G M times R O of the input in parallel with R O of the load.
Input C M: floor V I S S plus V G S 1 for both. Ceiling: with current-source loads V D D minus V overdrive 3 plus V threshold N; with the diode of the 5-T, V D D minus V G S 3 plus V threshold 1.
Fully differential swing: twice V D D minus three overdrives.
5-T swing: no factor two, single output.
Input C M range: floor is the tail check plus a link, ceiling is the load plus the fence. Swing: V D D minus the blocks in the output column.
Lecture 2: the two one-stage op amps. For each, four numbers: gain, input C M range, swing, bandwidth.
5-T: A. V equals G M 2 ( R O 2 in parallel with R O 4 ), C M max V D D minus V G S 3 plus V threshold 1.
Fully differential swing: 2( V D D minus V overdrive 3 minus V overdrive 1 minus V I S S ).
As a buffer the 5-T output resistance falls to 1 over G M 2 and its pole moves up to G M 2 over C L.
Telescopic gain: about g M r O, squared over 2.
Fully differential telescopic swing: twice V D D minus five blocks.
With a diode-stack mirror, one whole V threshold P is lost.
As a buffer the telescopic only works in a window V threshold minus V overdrive 4 wide.
Telescopic used as a buffer: two fences, M 4 gives the floor and M 2 the ceiling.
Lecture 3: the 5-T as a unity-gain buffer, then the telescopic op amp and its narrow buffer window.
Telescopic: A. is about g M r O, squared over 2.
Buffer window: V B 1 minus V threshold 4 to V B 1 minus V G S 4 plus V threshold 2.
0.316 volts.

1.8 minus 0.7 plus 0.4: 1.5 volts.
Five blocks of 0.2: 1.6 volts peak to peak.

One: the power gives the current; each side gets half the tail.
Two: the swing budget. What is left of V D D is shared among the stacked overdrives.
Three: sizes from the square law.
Four: check the gain with the two looks.
Five: not enough gain? Make the loads longer: G M R O grows with root WL over I D, while the overdrives stay put.
Any design question: write the five steps down first, then fill in numbers.
Lecture 4: the design recipe. Every design question follows the same order.
Design order: currents, overdrives, sizes, gain, lengthen.
Example 9.6: the output C M is V B minus ( V G S 3, 4 minus V threshold 1, 2 ).
K C L at the fold: each bottom source carries the cascode branch plus half the tail.
Looking up: an ordinary P mos cascode.
Looking down: two R O hang on the fold node, R O 1 and R O 9.
Gain: G M 1 times the two looks in parallel.
Currents in a folded cascode: bottom source equals branch plus half the tail. Gain: remember the two R O at the fold node.
Lecture 5: folding takes the input device out of the output column.
R down equals G M 3 R O 3 ( R O 1 in parallel with R O 9 ).
Bottom source equals I branch plus I S S over 2.
P mos input: floor V overdrive 9 minus V threshold P, below ground; ceiling V D D minus V overdrive 11 minus V G S 1.
N mos input: floor V overdrive 11 plus V G S 1; ceiling V D D minus V overdrive 10 plus V threshold 1, above V D D.
Rail-to-rail: both pairs; G M doubles in the middle.
Folded buffer: two floors, the higher binds, no ceiling from the input device.
Diode-stack load: a whole V threshold P is lost.
Low-voltage cascode load: V B sits between two fences, and no diode tax.
Folded input range: it passes the rail opposite to the input pair. Bias limits: a source at its edge, then a link.

P mos input floor V overdrive 9 minus V threshold P; N mos input ceiling V D D minus V overdrive 10 plus V threshold 1.
1 milliamp in total, 0.5 per side.
1 milliamp.

2 volts, above V D D.

(W over L) of an N mos carrying that current (0.5 milliamps)?
Folded cascode: current in each bottom current source?

N mos-input folded cascode: highest input common-mode level?
Two stages: the gains multiply.
Stage 1 telescopic: the two cascode looks.
Stage 2, a common-source: G M 9 times R O 9 in parallel with R O 11.
The D C level between the stages is a link: V D D minus V G S 9.
Boosting: an amplifier holding the source multiplies the output resistance by (1 plus A. 1 ).
Two-stage: multiply the gains, find X by a link. Auxiliary amplifier: multiply the cascode term by one plus A. 1.
Lecture 7: two stages split the jobs, and the first gain-boosting result.
A. equals A. 1 A. 2, V X equals V D D minus V G S 9.
R out equals R S plus R O plus (1 plus A. 1 ) G M R S R O.
Boosted cascode: G M is still G M 1; R out gains a factor (1 plus A. 1 ).
So the gain is about ( G M R O ) cubed.
A CS booster: A. 1 equals G M 3 R O 3, but X sits at V G S 3: the output floor is V G S 3 plus V overdrive 2.
A P mos booster forces V G S 2 is at most V threshold 3: M 2 barely on. It fails.
The folded booster: A. 1 equals G M 3 G M 4 R O 3 R O 4, no swing lost.
Boosted cascode: (1 plus A. 1 ) G M 2 R O 2 R O 1. Lowest output with a CS booster: V G S 3 plus V overdrive 2.
Lecture 8: the full boosted cascode, and the three ways to build the booster.
R out is about (1 plus A. 1 ) G M 2 R O 2 R O 1.
CS booster: V out, min equals V G S 3 plus V overdrive 2.
With the folded booster: G M 1 times one plus the booster gain times the cascode.
Differential CS booster: check, link, check: V I S S 1 plus V G S 5 plus V overdrive 3.
A whole folded cascode as booster: its gain by two looks.
Low nodes need P mos-input boosters; high nodes need N mos-input ones.
Why C M F B: a tiny current mismatch times a huge resistance moves the output C M to a rail.
Which input pair: look at the D C level. C M drift: the mismatch current times R P parallel R N.
Lecture 9: the booster is just another amplifier, and a fully differential op amp needs C M F B.
delta V out, C M equals ( I P minus I N )( R P in parallel with R N ).
Low cascodes: P mos-input booster. High cascodes: N mos-input.

50 times 51 times 50: about 127 thousand. That is ( G M R O ) cubed.

Half a volt from one microamp: that is why C M F B.
Boosting multiplies, and every booster costs a little headroom.
Two-stage op amp: total open-loop gain?
Gain of the boosted cascode stage?
Cascode with a CS booster: lowest output voltage?
Fully differential output: how far does the output C M move because of the mismatch?
Any two signals: the average is C M, the difference is D M.
C M F B: sense the output C M, compare with V ref, correct a current source.
Two resistors average the outputs, but they load them: R 1 appears in parallel in the gain.
Source followers do not load the outputs, but shift the level by V G S and cost swing.
The C M F B loop gain: error-amp gain, times G M of the corrected device, times the output resistance.
Sensing resistors: put them in parallel in the gain. C M F B loop gain: sense, amplify, current, resistance.

Resistive sensing: A. V equals G M 1 ( R O 1 in parallel with R O 3 in parallel with R 1 ).
C M F B: sense, compare with V ref, correct.
